claims.text: Adding SiC to ZrB2 lowers the required preparation temperature.
Adding SiC to ZrB2 reduces porosity.
Adding SiC reduces hole formation during prolonged exposure to liquid plating baths.
SiC promotes liquid-phase sintering of ZrB2.
SiC improves grain-boundary cohesion in ZrB2.
ZrB2 containing 5 vol% SiC can be sintered at 1900–2000 °C under an inert atmosphere.
The SiC addition produces a ZrB2–SiC composite microstructure with enhanced grain-boundary connectivity.
The ZrB2–SiC composite microstructure has reduced porosity.
SiC inhibits grain growth during sintering of ZrB2.
Lower-temperature liquid-phase sintering and inhibited grain growth produce a denser microstructure with fewer defects.
Improved grain-boundary cohesion and reduced porosity limit penetration of the plating liquid.
Limiting plating-liquid infiltration reduces hole formation.
ZrB2 with 5 vol% SiC sintered at 1900–2000 °C will achieve density similar to or higher than single-phase ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
After plating-bath exposure, the ZrB2–SiC composite will have fewer holes than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
After plating-bath exposure, the ZrB2–SiC composite will retain greater structural integrity than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
The ZrB2–SiC composite will have a lower component failure rate than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 typically has higher porosity than the proposed ZrB2–SiC composite.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 develops more holes during plating-bath exposure than the proposed composite.
The hypothesis applies to ZrB2 ceramics containing no more than 10 vol% SiC and prepared at 1900–2000 °C.
The proposed service boundary is plating-bath exposure for up to 100 hours at temperatures no higher than 80 °C.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as single-phase ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C, but the experimental control is specified as sintered at exactly 2300 °C.
